title: Insert a Node at the Tail of a Linked List
directAnswer: If the list is empty, the new node IS the head — return it. Otherwise walk to the last node (the one whose next is null) and set its next to the new node, then return the original head. O(n) time without a tail pointer, O(1) with one.

remember.pattern: Walk to the tail, then link; special-case the empty list
remember.formula:
newNode = ListNode(data)
if head is None:
    return newNode
cur = head
while cur.next is not None:
    cur = cur.next
cur.next = newNode
return head
rules: **Empty list is the special case**: return the new node as the head — you can't dereference a null head.
Walk with the guard `while cur.next != null` — stop *on* the last node, not past it.
Set `tail.next = newNode`; the new node's next is already null (it's the new tail).
**Return the original head** for a non-empty list — appending doesn't change the head.
Without a tail pointer this is O(n); keep a tail reference if you append repeatedly to get O(1).
whenToUse: Append to the back of a singly linked list, preserving insertion order (FIFO build-up)
Building a list front-to-back as elements arrive
Implementing a queue's enqueue when you maintain a tail pointer
Any 'add to end' on a structure without random access to the last element
antiSignals: You append in a tight loop and care about speed → keep a tail pointer for O(1) per append
You insert at the front → that's head insertion, O(1) with no walk
You insert at a known index → walk to position − 1 and splice (insert at position)
remember.takeaway: Tail insertion has two cases: empty list (new node becomes head) and non-empty (walk to the last node and link). The walk is what makes it O(n); a maintained tail pointer collapses it to O(1) and turns this into a queue's enqueue.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you handle the empty-list case (return the new node), use the correct walk guard to land on the last node, and know that appending leaves the head unchanged.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Dereferencing a null head, walking with `while cur != null` (overshooting past the tail to null), or returning the new node instead of the original head for a non-empty list.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call out the empty-list branch up front, note it's O(n) without a tail pointer, and mention that maintaining a tail makes it O(1) — exactly how a linked-list queue enqueues.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `data`.

Create a **new node** holding `data` and insert it at the **end** of the list, so it becomes the new tail. Return *the head of the modified list*.

If the list is empty, the new node becomes the head.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
Without a tail pointer, the append is O(n)
understanding: Appending puts the new node after every existing node. For a non-empty list we must find the current last node (its next is null) and point it at the new node. For an empty list there is nothing to walk, so the new node simply becomes the head.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens if the list is empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The new node becomes the head and is returned. You must branch on this because you can't walk a null head.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have a tail pointer available?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Plain version doesn't — so we walk to the end in O(n). If a tail pointer is maintained, appending is O(1).

clarifyingQuestions.question: What do I return for a non-empty list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The original head. Appending changes the tail, not the head, so the head reference is unchanged.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the new node need its next set?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It defaults to null, which is correct — the appended node is the new tail and points at nothing.

examples.explanation: Walk to node 3 (next is null), set 3.next = new node 4. Head stays at node 1.
Empty list: the new node 9 becomes the head and is returned.
Node 5 is already the tail (5.next is null); set 5.next = 8. Return head (node 5).

approaches.name: Walk to the Tail and Link (Optimal without a tail pointer)
approaches.whenToMention: The standard answer. Open with the empty-list branch, then the walk, and state it's O(n) without a maintained tail.
hints: The new node has to come after every current node. If the list is empty, there's nothing to come after — what should you return?
For a non-empty list, you need the last node: the one whose next is null. How do you walk to it?
Use a pointer and loop `while cur.next != null`. When it stops, cur is the tail — set cur.next to the new node and return the original head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: We may traverse all n nodes to reach the tail → O(n) time. A new node plus one walking pointer → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Build the new node, handle the empty list, then walk to the last node and attach.

**The empty-list branch comes first.** If `head` is null there's no node to attach to, and trying to walk it would dereference null. So we return the new node immediately — it becomes the sole element and the head. This branch is mandatory, unlike head insertion where the empty case folds into the general path.

**Walking to the tail.** For a non-empty list we start `cur = head` and advance while `cur.next != null`. The guard is the subtle part: we want to *stop on* the last node, not run off the end. When `cur.next` is null, `cur` is the tail. If we had looped on `while cur != null`, `cur` would end up null and we'd have nowhere to attach.

**Linking and returning.** Set `cur.next = newNode`. The new node's `next` is already null by construction, so it correctly becomes the new tail. We return the *original* head because appending never moves the head — only head insertion does that.

**Why this is O(n).** Reaching the tail means visiting every node. Repeated appends each pay O(n), so building a list of n elements this way is O(n²). The fix is a maintained tail pointer (see insight), which makes each append O(1).
approaches.insight: If you keep a separate `tail` pointer alongside `head`, appending becomes `tail.next = newNode; tail = newNode` — O(1), no walk. That's exactly how a linked-list-backed queue enqueues. The walk-to-tail version is what you write when only the head is given.

Link the old tail to the new node.

Empty-list branch returns the new node as head.
Advance until cur is the last node.
Attach the new node to the tail.
Return the original head — the front of the list didn't move.

pitfalls: Not handling the empty list — dereferencing head.next when head is null throws.
Looping on `while cur != null` — cur ends at null with nowhere to attach.
Returning newNode instead of the original head for a non-empty list.
Appending in a loop without a tail pointer — O(n) each time, O(n²) overall.

edgeCases.behavior: head is null → return the new node as the head → [9].
cur.next is null immediately → 5.next = 8; return head → [5, 8].

commonMistakes: Forgetting the empty-list branch and dereferencing a null head.
Using `while cur != null` so cur overshoots the tail to null.
Returning the new node instead of the original head for a non-empty list.
Repeated tail appends without a tail pointer, making list construction O(n²).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Crashing on the empty list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If head is null, the walk loop immediately reads head.next (or cur.next) on a null reference and throws. The empty list must short-circuit by returning the new node.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overshooting the tail
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Guarding on `while cur is not None` advances cur all the way to None, so there is no node left to attach the new node to.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cur = head
while cur is not None:   # cur ends up None
    cur = cur.next
cur.next = new_node      # AttributeError: None has no .next
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cur = head
while cur.next is not None:   # stop on the last node
    cur = cur.next
cur.next = new_node
